name: Halo laser (hybrid fractional)

lead: Halo is a hybrid fractional laser that combines two wavelengths in a single treatment. People use it to get a more even skin tone and smoother texture, and to soften sun damage, pigment and scars.

It works by creating microscopic columns of controlled injury, one set shallow and one deeper, which the skin heals by remodeling. Registered studies are small: a 15-person study of facial and neck photoaging, a 34-person study of conditions including dyschromia and photodamage, and a trial of a hybrid fractional laser for acne scars in skin of color.

paras: Halo is done in a dermatology or aesthetic clinic, usually as a single session or a short series. Downtime depends on how deep the settings are set, so people plan recovery around the chosen intensity. Results build as skin remodels over the following weeks.

Hyperpigmentation after laser treatment is a studied concern, particularly in darker skin tones. Redness, swelling and peeling occur while skin heals, and downtime varies with settings. It is a clinic-only procedure, and people with active skin infections or a tendency to scar should raise that with the provider.

chain: Even tone, smoother scars and texture
angle.text: Halo combines ablative and non-ablative wavelengths in one pass so skin resurfaces at two depths and remodels, evening tone and smoothing scars and texture. People use it for sun damage, scars and pigment, and registered studies of 15 to 34 people have examined it.

lead: Halo is a hybrid fractional laser, a category that combines an ablative and a non-ablative fractional wavelength in a single pass, aimed at photoaging, scars and pigment [1][2]. People use it in clinics to improve skin texture, tone and fine lines, and to soften scarring, so that the skin looks smoother and more even.

In the hybrid system described in the published multicenter trial, a 1470 nm wavelength creates controlled zones of coagulation in the dermis while a 2940 nm wavelength vaporises tissue in the epidermis, with both delivered in one fractional treatment [3]. The idea behind fractional lasers in general is to treat a grid of tiny zones and leave islands of healthy skin between them, which was thought to speed healing [4].

Review articles describe hybrid fractional lasers as one option on a spectrum from full-field ablative resurfacing, which remains the choice for some patients with extensive photodamage and lighter skin, to non-ablative devices with less downtime [5][6]. Published and registered studies of the hybrid devices are small, and are summarised below.
infobox: Photoaging, dyschromia, acne scars, skin laxity, actinic keratoses
Typical sessions in a published trial

paras: Fractional photothermolysis was developed to create many microscopic thermal injury columns rather than injuring the whole skin surface, which shortens recovery and widens the range of skin types and body sites that can be treated [4]. Fractionation was first used with non-ablative lasers and later applied to ablative, picosecond and hybrid devices, as well as to radiofrequency [4].

A hybrid fractional system sequentially uses two wavelengths. In the multicenter study, the 1470 nm beam is absorbed by water and produces zones of coagulation to depths up to 700 micrometres in the dermis, while the 2940 nm beam is highly absorbed by water and ablates the epidermis to about 110 micrometres [3]. The authors described the aim as improving pigmentation, tone, texture and other features of photoaging [3].

Studies of the hybrid laser address facial and neck photoaging, dyschromia and photodamage, acne scarring, and off-face skin laxity [1][2][7][8]. A review of laser resurfacing says erbium, carbon dioxide and ablative, non-ablative and hybrid fractional lasers are popular tools in plastic surgery and dermatology offices [9].
A letter in Dermatologic Surgery reports hybrid fractional resurfacing of actinic keratoses, and registered studies are testing 1470 nm treatment in scarring and androgenetic alopecia [10][11][12].

In an open-label multicenter study of 34 women with Fitzpatrick skin types I to IV (mean age 52), each had two treatments four to six weeks apart and were followed for three months. Among the 29 who completed it, blinded evaluators found significant improvement in 80%, the average pain score was 4 out of 10, and all respondents reported satisfaction with results [3].

Reviews note that multiple treatments may be required with fractional devices, and that some results of hybrid and non-ablative devices may be duplicated by well-established intense pulsed light, according to one 2018 review [6]. The same review says full-field ablative resurfacing remains the procedure of choice for people with lighter skin and extensive photodamage and wrinkles [6].

The multicenter study reported two cases of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation that resolved within 90 days and no other adverse events [3]. Hyperpigmentation after laser is the focus of a registered trial in skin of colour with acne scars [7]. The recovery period involves swelling, redness and roughness, which a small split-face trial of a peptide gel and a randomised pair of studies of a post-procedure cream aimed to reduce [13][14].

The multicenter open-label trial described above enrolled 34 women and is the most detailed published study of the hybrid system [3]. A completed study registered in 2015 evaluated the Profile Halo mixed fractional laser for facial and neck photoaging in 15 participants [1]. A completed 2016 study (n=34) addressed dyschromia and photodamaged skin [2]. A 2019 study tested a hybrid fractional laser on off-face skin laxity in 7 participants [8], and a recruiting trial from 2023 (n=50) examines acne scars with pigmentation risk in skin of colour [7].

Recovery products have also been studied after hybrid laser. A single-centre randomised split-face study in five subjects found less redness on postoperative days 1 and 4 and less roughness on days 3 and 4 with a peptide gel plus regimen [13]. Two randomised, double-blinded split-face studies in women aged 35 to 65 (16 completing after hybrid laser, 22 after fractional CO2 laser) found a post-procedure cream performed similarly to or better than conventional routines on erythema, edema and discomfort; the authors noted the small samples [14]. A registered 20-person study of procedure pairing with a hybrid fractional laser for facial rejuvenation has completed [15].

Studies of hybrid fractional lasers in other fields include a randomised, placebo-controlled trial in 31 postmenopausal women of radiofrequency and a hybrid fractional laser for vulvovaginal symptoms, which reported improvements in symptom scores at three months [16].

Registered work includes a terminated five-person study of fractional photothermolysis for hair follicle induction and recruiting studies of a 1470 nm laser for androgenetic and scarring alopecia [11][12]. Reviews describe hybrid and fractional devices as an expanding category whose applications now reach more skin types and body sites [4].
